newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Coast CEO sees in-market mergers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Coast CEO sees in-market mergers.

text.p: Coast Savings Financial Inc chief executive officer Ray Martin said he expects to see more marriages among California's thrifts.
"I think we'll see more in-market consolidations. Some people view this as defensive, but in-market consolidations offer a lot of advantages," he said.

Martin declined comment on rumors Coast was in merger talks with Washington Mutual Savings Bank or other thrifts. "It's all rumors, and we don't discuss rumors," he told Reuters in an interview this week.

"There's been a lot of merger activity in California. It's long been anticipated and is now starting to materialize. People are assuming Coast will be next. It might be realized or it might not," he said.

Coast, with $8.2 billion in assets, has long topped the list of commonly-named takeover candidates in California following a recent wave of mergers, including Wells Fargo and Co's purchase of First Interstate Bancorp Inc, Washington Mutual's acquisition of American Savings Bank of Irvine and First Nationwide Bank's merger with California Federal Bancorp Inc.
Both Washington Mutual and First Nationwide have stated their plans to further expand in California.
Several industry sources at the Western League of Savings Institutions convention in Santa Barbara, Calif., this week cited rumors that Coast was talking with various parties.
"My responsibility is to preserve and increase shareholder value and if we were to accomplish that through an acquisition or by being acquired, we would entertain that," Martin said.
Several analysts said the merger wave may cool for six to nine months until Washington Mutual and First Nationwide absorb their recent acquisitions.

Analysts also said further mergers with out-of-state acquirers may slow in the short-term as executives of target thrifts hold out for premium prices. The average price to deposit ratios of these transactions range from four percent to eight percent, analysts said.

"Everybody on Wall Street will tell you that everybody's on the radar screen," said Martin, adding, "If you've got three to four people going after the same group of prospects, prices will naturally go higher."
Nevertheless, Martin said companies are worth different prices to different buyers.
For instance, he said, "an in-market consolidation may afford a higher premium, because of (easier to accomplish) cost savings."
